levels.title: Who Looks at Whom
levels.story: A note on the lookout says: 'The owl saw the fox because it was hungry.' Wren frowns. "Who was hungry, the owl or the fox?" Kit points at the owl. "How do you know?" Wren asks. "I looked back over the sentence and weighed each word."

everyday.scene: In a crowded room, you decide who to listen to by how relevant they are, not by who is closest.
everyday.question: How can a program decide which other words matter for understanding one word?
everyday.answer: It gives every other word a score, turns the scores into weights, and blends the words using those weights. This is attention, the core of a transformer.

lessons.title: Weighing the other words
text: Attention lets each word look at every other word and decide how much each one matters. The word gets a score for each of them, and a function called softmax turns the scores into weights that are positive and add up to 1.
In 'the owl saw the fox because it was hungry', the word 'it' might give owl 67 percent, fox 24 percent and 'the' 9 percent. The new meaning of 'it' is then a blend of the words, mostly owl.

terms.meaning: Weighing how much each word matters for another word.
Turns scores into positive weights that add up to 1.

lessons.title: Looking at everything at once
text: A transformer applies attention to every word of a sentence at the same time. In June 2017 a paper called 'Attention Is All You Need' proposed a network built only from attention, with no recurrence. It was more parallelisable and faster to train.
Attention alone does not know word order, so transformers add position information to each word. Without it, 'owl saw fox' and 'fox saw owl' would look the same.

predict.prompt: A word has scores 1, 1, 1 and 1 for four words. What weight does each get?
predict.answer: 25 percent each, because equal scores give equal weights.

lessons.title: The price of looking everywhere
text: Every word compares itself with every other word, so a text of n words needs n times n comparisons. Eight words need 64. One hundred words need 10,000. Double the text and the work grows fourfold.
Standard self-attention has costs that grow quadratically with the sequence length. That is why very long texts are expensive, and why researchers keep looking for cheaper variants.

deeper.title: Parallel versus recurrent
text: An RNN must finish one word before starting the next. A transformer can handle all words at once during training, which suits modern graphics hardware.

fieldNotes.title: Attention
fieldNotes.text: Attention is a method that determines the importance of each component in a sequence relative to the other components in that sequence.

fieldNotes.title: Transformers
fieldNotes.text: The transformer was introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need'. It uses attention instead of recurrence and is easier to run in parallel.

fieldNotes.title: Cost
fieldNotes.text: Standard self-attention has computational and memory costs that grow quadratically with sequence length.

summary: You gave each word a score for every other word, turned scores into weights, blended the words, and saw why attention gets expensive on long texts.
Wren reads the note again. "It was the owl that was hungry. You weighed every word, and the owl won."

mistake.title: Thinking weights are rules
mistake.text: The weights come from learned scores, not fixed rules. The numbers in this level are made up to show the idea, and a real model computes them for each sentence.
